name: Tomas Schmidt

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. This is confidential. What happens on an ordinary workday?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m 43 and was promoted six months ago to manage five people who sort disputed invoices at a large food distributor. I check the overnight claims, assign the ones with missing delivery records and try to keep a promised reply from slipping. I use AI every day to line up invoice numbers and draft a first response, though I still miss things my experienced clerk catches. I like calling a small buyer and finally getting their bill right; I hate holding the team late because I misjudged the queue.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is home like, and what room do you have if your pay changes?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner, Eva, works at the school kitchen, and our children are eight and eleven. We have a mortgage, less than a month of expenses saved and no spare room in my lower-than-usual manager pay. I finished a bachelor’s degree years ago but only recently learned to lead a team; I’m still slower than the other managers. There are few similar offices nearby, so I keep trying new tools because I need to get better here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell my team that the matching tool helps us find a number, but someone must still call the buyer about a disputed delivery. I’d keep the clerk’s final check on my replies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The job probably stays, which is good. The mortgage and Eva’s short school breaks still make a thin month frightening, even if AI does little.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tomorrow I’d keep the daily claim list and ask my clerk to review the two types of invoice error I miss most. In the first year I’d continue using the matching tool and put 25 a month into emergency savings only when Eva’s school wages arrive in full.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m anxious about our money, even with the job holding. A small repair bill could still put us behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What bill would you worry about first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The boiler would be the one. If it broke in winter, the mortgage payment would still arrive on its usual date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does asking the clerk to check your work feel awkward?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little, because I’m the manager. I’d rather admit a missed delivery slip than send another wrong bill to a buyer.

say: I’d keep a **clerk’s final check** on disputed replies.
The matching tool helps find **invoice numbers**, not settle delivery arguments.
think: My **job likely holds** in a plateau.
The **mortgage and school breaks** still threaten our thin budget.
A **boiler repair** could still collide with the mortgage payment.
do: Keep the **daily claim list** and ask for a check on my common errors.
Save **25 monthly** only when Eva’s school wages arrive in full.
feel: I feel **anxious** about money despite steady work.
S0.quote: I’d rather admit a missed delivery slip than send another wrong bill to a buyer.
fieldNote: His current job appears **steady**, but the household has almost no reserve.
He uses **AI daily** yet openly relies on an experienced clerk.
A **boiler repair** could compete directly with the mortgage.

steps.text: Keep the daily claims list and clerk check on disputed invoice replies
Transfer 25 monthly to emergency savings only when Eva’s school wages arrive in full

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say invoice checking and written replies are exactly the work AI is taking. I’d ask our staff committee to see the trial numbers and any plan to cut posts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m the newest and weakest manager in the office, so a smaller claims team could mean my job goes first. I’m quick with the tool, but speed does not make me as good as the managers who know every customer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I’d test the new claims tool on fifty old disputes and count wrong delivery matches with the clerk. In the first year I’d take the paid company course on audit trails, then ask the staff committee to press for a funded transfer path if posts are cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed, because I can picture my name on the short list. I still want to run the test rather than let a vendor tell us it is safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you tell at home first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell Eva before the next mortgage payment, not after a rumour becomes a letter. We would need to know whether her kitchen hours can cover food for a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you say the tool is bad if it works well?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I would publish the errors and the staffing question together; the team deserves both numbers.

say: I’d ask for **trial numbers** and a staffing plan.
Invoice checks and replies are the **first exposed tasks**.
think: My **junior manager post** could go when claims shrink.
Daily tool use does not replace **customer judgment** I am still learning.
do: Test **fifty old disputes** with the clerk this month.
Complete a **paid audit course** and seek a funded transfer path through the committee.
feel: I feel **alarmed** about being first on a cut list.
S1.quote: I would publish the errors and the staffing question together; the team deserves both numbers.
fieldNote: He links **tool quality** to honest staffing discussion.
His low standing makes a **manager cut** feel personal and near.
The audit course is **paid**, and any transfer depends on funding.

steps.text: Test AI delivery matches against fifty past invoice disputes
Complete the paid company course on claims audit trails
Ask the staff committee to press for a funded transfer path

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell colleagues to keep copies of their work records and ask for a joint meeting about severance. The company should not leave each person to bargain alone with an automated portal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AGI in 2028 could do my checking, replying and assigning as well as I can, probably better. Robots for physical delivery work follow around 2031, so Eva’s kitchen work may last longer, but her wage will not carry the mortgage and two children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tonight Eva and I would list the mortgage, food and school costs and stop the weekend sports trips. Before 2028 I’d join the staff committee’s request for paid training and enroll in a warehouse equipment course only if the company covers the fee and hours; in the first year after AGI, I’d apply for an open depot floor role only if its wage covers the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m alarmed, almost sick with it. I can make a list, but two years is too short to build a cushion and learn a physical job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why depot work if robots arrive in 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It may buy our family a few paychecks while I learn something else. I know the hands-on work is not a permanent shelter in this picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the floor role pays less than the mortgage needs?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep searching and ask the committee about any transition pay. I will not keep my partner and two children fed with a hopeful job title.

say: Workers should keep **work records** before the 2028 change.
The team should not face an **automated portal** alone.
think: Eva’s school kitchen pay cannot cover **mortgage and children** alone.
Less than a month saved leaves almost **no search time**.
do: Stop **weekend sports trips** after reviewing bills with Eva.
Seek **funded warehouse training** and a posted floor role only at mortgage-covering pay.
feel: I feel **alarmed** by the two-year deadline.
S2.quote: I will not keep my partner and two children fed with a hopeful job title.
fieldNote: The **2028 thinking change** threatens his whole claims-management routine.
He treats depot work as a **bridge** before 2031 robots.
Training needs **paid fees and hours**; the floor wage must cover the mortgage.

steps.text: Stop weekend sports trips after reviewing the mortgage and school costs with Eva
Join the staff committee request for paid training and transition terms
Enroll in warehouse equipment training only if the company pays fees and hours
Apply for an open depot floor role after 2028 only if pay covers the mortgage

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say the company has five years to put paid training and real internal vacancies on the table. I’d ask the committee to check the numbers each year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might be able to become a stronger manager before the 2031 thinking system arrives, but that still may not save this job. Depot work would face robots around 2034, so I would need an actual offer, not just a course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting next term I’d enroll in a company-funded equipment certificate if Eva agrees we can manage the evening childcare. I’d ask our depot manager about posted floor vacancies before 2031 and apply only if the pay covers the mortgage; in the first year after AGI, I’d stay in the floor role only while there is paid hands-on work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m anxious, with enough time to test a course. Five years would help our children adjust if I changed shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if evening childcare costs more than the course is worth?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would postpone enrollment until the company offers paid daytime training. Eva already covers the school pickup when my claims queue runs late.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the children about a shift change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell them I might miss some weekday dinners but would be home for breakfast. I would not promise a new job until an employer puts the wage in writing.

say: I’d ask for **paid training** and posted vacancies.
The committee should review the **staffing numbers** each year.
An internal transfer needs **written wages** before anyone relies on it.
think: Becoming better at management may not save **this role**.
Depot jobs also face **2034 robots**, so an offer matters.
do: Enroll in a **funded equipment certificate** if childcare works.
Apply for **posted depot work** only at mortgage-covering pay and stay while hands-on work is paid.
feel: I feel **anxious**, with time to try a course.
S3.quote: I would not promise a new job until an employer puts the wage in writing.
fieldNote: He makes evening training depend on **Eva’s childcare agreement**.
He checks **actual depot vacancies** before counting on a move.
He sees **2034 robots** as a later risk to physical work.

steps.text: Enroll in company-funded equipment training only if Eva agrees evening childcare works
Apply for posted depot floor work before 2031 only if pay covers the mortgage
Keep the depot role after 2031 only while paid hands-on work remains

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say ten years is time for a proper agreement on training and job changes, not a reason to postpone it. The company should tell families which posts go and when.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could pay down the mortgage a little and get better at managing while we still have this work. I’d be 53 when thinking AI arrives in 2036; starting again then with little saved would be hard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This January I’d set up a 40 monthly emergency transfer if Eva’s school hours hold and ask the staff committee for a yearly transition meeting. I’d take the company’s paid supervision course next year and apply for an open depot operations role before 2036 only if its wage covers our mortgage; in the first year after AGI, I’d stay there only while the company funds paid human floor work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m anxious but more able to plan than in the two-year picture. Ten years might let us replace the thin cushion before any job changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you put the extra money into the mortgage or savings first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Savings first, because a boiler repair cannot be paid with a small reduction in the loan balance. I’d make mortgage overpayments later if the emergency account grows.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make the yearly meeting useful?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dates, course places and the number of actual depot openings, written down. Families cannot budget from a speech about opportunity.

say: I’d seek a **written transition agreement** now.
Families need **post dates** while there is time to adjust.
The company should count **actual openings**, not just course places.
think: I need a **larger cushion** before age 53.
Better management skills may help now, though **2036 AGI** still threatens the role.
do: Save **40 monthly** if Eva’s school hours hold.
Take a **paid supervision course** and apply only for mortgage-covering depot vacancies.
Stay in **depot operations** after 2036 only while paid human floor work remains.
feel: I feel **anxious** but able to build savings.
S4.quote: Families cannot budget from a speech about opportunity.
fieldNote: His first priority is **cash savings**, before mortgage overpayments.
He will be **53 in 2036** and wants savings before changing work.
His depot plan depends on **paid training** and a viable vacancy.

steps.text: Transfer 40 monthly to emergency savings while Eva’s school hours hold
Ask the staff committee for annual written transition meetings
Complete the company-paid supervision course next year
Apply for an open depot operations role before 2036 only if pay covers the mortgage

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most, because our mortgage and children will not wait while I change work. Paid training, written wages on real depot vacancies and a joint severance agreement would help. I can learn fast, but I cannot make Eva’s school wages cover everything.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask how a manager tells five people that a tool he tested may take their posts. I would rather show my team the bad matches and the staffing numbers in the same meeting.

headlineQuote: I would rather show my team the bad matches and the staffing numbers in the same meeting.
portrait: **Tomas**, 43, is a recently promoted invoice-claims manager with a bachelor’s degree.
His lower pay and **thin savings** strain a mortgage and two children.
He uses **AI daily**, though he still relies on an experienced clerk.
He seeks **paid training** and staff involvement before considering depot work.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove his thinking-heavy role before his family builds savings.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid training**, written wages for real depot openings and joint severance terms would support a move.
